title: Total probability theorem（全機率定理）
source_quote: Let A1 , . . . , An be disjoint events that form a partition of the sample space (each possible outcome is included in exactly one of the events A1 , . . . , An ) and assume that P(Ai ) > 0, for all i. Then, for any event B, we have P(B) = P(A1 )P(B | A1 ) + · · · + P(An )P(B | An ).
irreducible_premises: A1, …, An are mutually exclusive (every pairwise intersection is empty)
A1, …, An are exhaustive (their union is Ω, and every outcome lies in exactly one of them)
P(Ai) > 0 holds for every i
Finite additivity of probability
The multiplication rule P(Ai ∩ B) = P(Ai) P(B | Ai)
derivation_chain: Because the partition is mutually exclusive and exhaustive, the event B is cut into the n pieces B ∩ A1, …, B ∩ An, which are themselves mutually exclusive
By additivity, P(B) equals the sum of the probabilities of these n pieces
Rewrite each piece using the multiplication rule as P(Ai) P(B | Ai)
Adding them up gives P(B) = Σ P(Ai) P(B | Ai): first compute the conditional probability case by case, then weight each case by the probability that it occurs
Use the partition premise to decompose B as the disjoint union (B ∩ A_1) ∪ (B ∩ A_2) ∪ (B ∩ A_3) ∪ ... — the shaded slices of the ellipse in the p08 figure.
Apply the additivity premise to that disjoint union: P(B) = Σ_i P(B ∩ A_i), the first handwritten line.
Rewrite each term with the multiplication rule premise: P(B ∩ A_i) = P(A_i) P(B | A_i), giving P(B) = Σ_i P(A_i) P(B | A_i), the boxed result.
Observe from the partition premise that Σ_i P(A_i) = 1, as annotated, so the coefficients are legitimate weights summing to one.

Conclude that P(B) is a convex combination — a weighted average — of the numbers P(B | A_i), hence always lies between the smallest and largest of them; on p06, P(B) = 0.05 × 0.99 + 0.95 × 0.10 = 0.1445 lies between 0.10 and 0.99.
assumptions: The partition must be both mutually exclusive and exhaustive; neither condition can be dropped
Every P(Ai) > 0, otherwise the conditional probability in that term is undefined
Each A_i used in the sum has P(A_i) > 0 so that P(B | A_i) is defined
The same event B is used in every conditional term
failure_modes: If the cases are not mutually exclusive (e.g. conditioning on "it rains" and "the temperature is below 10 degrees"), the overlap is counted twice and the sum exceeds the true value
If the cases are not exhaustive, the remaining scenarios are omitted and the sum falls short of the true value; the probability of the missing piece is exactly the error bound
When some P(Ai) = 0 that term's conditional probability is undefined, so the zero-probability pieces must be removed before the formula can be applied
If the partition is not exhaustive, the sum only covers B ∩ (∪A_i) and understates P(B) by exactly P(B ∩ (∪A_i)^c) — the omitted slice is the error.
If the A_i overlap, the shared region B ∩ A_i ∩ A_j is counted twice and the sum can exceed 1, producing a 'probability' that is not a probability.

Averaging the conditionals with equal weights instead of weights P(A_i) gives the wrong answer whenever the partition is unbalanced: on p06 the unweighted mean (0.99 + 0.10)/2 = 0.545 versus the correct 0.1445, a nearly four-fold overstatement because the rare cause A has weight only 0.05.

title: Why conditional probability（條件機率）is a new probability law（機率律）
source_quote: The conditional probability of an event A, given an event B with P(B) > 0, is defined by P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), and specifies a new (conditional) probability law on the same sample space Ω.
irreducible_premises: The original probability law P is already defined on the sample space Ω and satisfies the three axioms of nonnegativity, normalization, and additivity
The event B satisfies P(B) > 0
The defining formula of conditional probability, P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), where dividing by P(B) serves to make the probability of B itself equal to 1
derivation_chain: Discard the part of A that does not lie inside B, so that only A ∩ B remains possible
The total remaining probability is then P(B), not 1, so the normalization axiom is violated
Renormalize by dividing through by P(B), which gives P(B | B) = 1 and restores normalization
Nonnegativity and additivity are preserved under division by a positive constant, so all three axioms hold
Hence P(· | B) is itself a complete probability law, and every theorem proved for the original law carries over unchanged
assumptions: P(B) > 0, otherwise the denominator of the defining formula is zero
B is a fixed event; once B changes you are working with a different probability law, and the two must not be mixed
failure_modes: When P(B) = 0, P(A | B) is undefined; single-point events for continuous random variables have probability zero, so the elementary definition cannot be used here and one must work with conditional densities instead

Misreading "conditional probability is a probability law" as "conditional probability and the original law are interchangeable": P(A | B) and P(A) belong to two different laws, and mixing them yields contradictory results

title: Why independence（獨立性）is defined by the product form rather than by P(A | B) = P(A)
source_quote: Two events A and B are said to be independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). If in addition, P(B) > 0, independence is equivalent to the condition P(A | B) = P(A).
irreducible_premises: The intuition independence is meant to capture is that the occurrence of B does not change our assessment of A
The conditional form P(A | B) = P(A) is only meaningful when P(B) > 0
The product form P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) is meaningful in every case
derivation_chain: If the conditional form were taken as the definition, events with P(B) = 0 could not be classified as independent or not, leaving a gap in the definition
The product form is fully symmetric in A and B, so there is no need to specify which event is conditioned on which
When P(B) > 0, dividing both sides of the product form by P(B) recovers P(A | B) = P(A), so the two are equivalent
Hence the product form is a strictly more general definition, and it delivers symmetry for free
Start from the informative statement P(B|A) = P(B), using the premise that this is the intended meaning of independence.
Substitute it into the multiplication rule P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A), which requires P(A) > 0, to obtain P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) — this is the handwritten chain P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B|A)=P(A)P(B) on the slide.

Promote the product form to the definition, using the premise that the product is defined for all events: it needs no positivity and is symmetric in A and B, so P(A|B) = P(A) follows for free whenever P(B) > 0.

Apply the nonnegativity premise to the slide's disjoint picture: A and B disjoint with P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0 give P(A∩B) = 0 while P(A)P(B) > 0, so disjointness is the opposite of independence rather than a version of it.
assumptions: The equivalence holds only when P(B) > 0; the product form itself requires no assumption that any probability be positive
A and B are events in a single, fixed probability model with one probability law
The conditional form is used only as motivation; all formal work uses the product form
Independence is a property of the assigned probabilities, not of any physical or causal mechanism
failure_modes: Mistaking mutual exclusivity for independence: if A and B are mutually exclusive with positive probabilities, then P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B), so mutual exclusivity is in fact the strongest form of dependence

Using "there is no actual causal link" as the test for independence: independence is a numerical condition on the probability law and has nothing to do with the presence or absence of physical causation

Treating 'A and B cannot happen together' as independence: for disjoint events with positive probability, P(A∩B)=0 but P(A)P(B)>0, so the product rule fails by exactly P(A)P(B) — the slide answers 'Independent?' with P(A∩B)=0 vs P(A)P(B)>0.
Using P(B|A)=P(B) as the definition when P(A)=0: the conditional is undefined and the test cannot be run, while the product form is satisfied trivially since both sides are 0.

Reading independence as causal or physical separateness: two events driven by the same source can still satisfy the product rule numerically, and two mechanically unrelated events can fail it, so any argument from 'unrelated mechanisms' can give the wrong answer.

title: Independence and conditional independence（條件獨立性）do not imply each other
source_quote: Independence does not imply conditional independence, and vice versa.
irreducible_premises: Conditional independence is defined as independence under the probability law P(· | C): P(A ∩ B | C) = P(A | C)P(B | C)
Independence is a property relative to one particular probability law
Changing what you condition on changes the law
derivation_chain: Independence is a numerical identity that holds under the law P, while conditional independence is an identity under the law P(· | C); the two live in different laws
Since these are two different laws, one holding is no reason for the other to hold, and both directions must be settled by counterexample

Counterexample (independent but not conditionally independent): two biased coins with P(H | coin A) = 0.9 and P(H | coin B) = 0.1; pick one coin at random with equal probability and then toss it repeatedly. When you do not know which coin was picked, the tosses are dependent (ten heads in a row sharply raises the probability that the next toss is heads), but given the identity of the coin the tosses are independent
Conclusion: conditioning can create dependence, and it can also remove dependence
Substitute P(·|C) for P(·) in the product-form definition, using the premise that independence is relative to a law: A ⟂ B given C means P(A∩B|C) = P(A|C)P(B|C).
Note that this identity and the unconditional identity P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) are statements about different laws, so by the rescaling premise neither implies the other.

Exhibit destruction with the slide's Venn picture: A and B independent unconditionally, but inside C the two shaded pieces of A and B no longer overlap in the same proportion, so P(A∩B|C) ≠ P(A|C)P(B|C).

Exhibit creation with the two-coin model on p06: tosses of the same unknown coin are dependent unconditionally, yet given the identity of the coin the tosses are independent — the annotation 'given a coin: independent tosses'.
Quantify the dependence by total probability: P(toss 11 = H) = P(A)P(H₁₁|A) + P(B)P(H₁₁|B) = 0.5·0.9 + 0.5·0.1 = 0.5, whereas P(toss 11 = H | first 10 tosses heads) ≈ P(H₁₁|A) = 0.9.
assumptions: P(C) > 0, otherwise P(· | C) is undefined
P(C) > 0 so that the conditional law exists
The conditioning variable is the same for both events in the pair
The mixture over the unobserved coin is nondegenerate — the two conditional coin biases differ
failure_modes: Wrongly assuming marginal independence in a mixture model (first draw a parameter, then draw the observations): this is exactly the source of error in Bayesian inference when observations are treated as independent samples
The reverse misuse: independence given C does not imply marginal independence

Assuming unconditional independence survives conditioning: in the slide's Venn diagram A and B are independent but disjoint inside C, so P(A∩B|C) = 0 while P(A|C)P(B|C) > 0 — the product rule fails by the whole of P(A|C)P(B|C).

Assuming conditional independence implies unconditional independence: in the two-coin model tosses are conditionally independent given the coin, yet observing 10 heads moves the eleventh-toss probability from 0.5 to about 0.9, an error of 0.4 in absolute probability from treating tosses as unconditionally independent.

Conditioning on a set that mixes regimes: if C is a union of sub-cases with different conditional biases, the conditional law is again a mixture and the product form fails even though it holds inside each sub-case.

title: Independence of several events（多事件獨立）must hold for every subset
source_quote: We say that the events A1 , A2 , . . . , An are independent if P( ∩ i∈S Ai ) = Π i∈S P(Ai ), for every subset S of {1, 2, . . . , n}.
irreducible_premises: The definition requires the identity to hold for every subset S of {1, …, n}, not merely for pairs
There are 2ⁿ subsets, so the number of conditions grows exponentially in n
derivation_chain: Pairwise independence constrains only the subsets of size 2 and imposes no constraint at all on subsets of size 3 or more
Hence there exist probability laws in which the events are pairwise independent but the three of them are not independent; pairwise independence is a strictly weaker condition

Counterexample: toss two fair coins and let A = the first is heads, B = the second is heads, C = the two outcomes agree. The three events are pairwise independent, yet P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = 1/4 ≠ 1/8 = P(A)P(B)P(C)
So to use the word "independent" you must check every subset, or guarantee it directly from the construction of the model (the experiments being physically separate)
assumptions: No additional positivity requirement; the definition is purely a product identity
failure_modes: Misusing pairwise independence to multiply out a system failure probability in reliability calculations systematically understates the risk from common-cause failures (shared power supply, shared data center, shared supplier)

title: Independence is closed under complements（補事件）
source_quote: If A and B are independent, so are A and B c .
irreducible_premises: A splits into the two mutually exclusive pieces (A ∩ B) and (A ∩ Bᶜ)
P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) holds
derivation_chain: By additivity, P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)
Substituting the independence condition gives P(A) − P(A)P(B) = P(A)(1 − P(B))
Since 1 − P(B) = P(Bᶜ), we get P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A)P(Bᶜ), that is, A and Bᶜ are independent
Intuitive version: if the occurrence of B carries no information about A, then the non-occurrence of B carries no information either
Decompose A into the two disjoint pieces A∩B and A∩Bᶜ, using the splitting premise.
Apply finite additivity: P(A) = P(A∩B) + P(A∩Bᶜ).
Substitute the independence hypothesis P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) and solve for the remaining piece: P(A∩Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A)P(B).
Factor P(A) out and apply the complement rule: P(A∩Bᶜ) = P(A)(1 − P(B)) = P(A)P(Bᶜ), which is the product form for A and Bᶜ.
assumptions: Only the independence of A and B is needed; no assumption that any probability be positive is required
A and B are independent under the same law used to evaluate the complement
The complement Bᶜ is taken inside the same sample space Ω
Only two events are involved; no claim about complements inside larger collections is made here
failure_modes: This property does not extend to "A independent of B and A independent of C ⇒ A independent of B ∪ C"; the latter requires additional conditions

Complementing under a different law: if the independence was only conditional independence given C, the algebra runs inside P(·|C) and yields P(A∩Bᶜ|C)=P(A|C)P(Bᶜ|C), which says nothing about the unconditional pair — the conclusion is silently attached to the wrong probability law.

Extending the same one-line argument to a collection assumed only pairwise independent: the substitution step needs the product identity for the exact intersection being split, and pairwise independence does not supply the three-way identity, so the derivation stalls at P(A₁∩A₂∩A₃ᶜ).

Applying it to disjointness instead of independence: if A and B are disjoint, A∩Bᶜ = A, and P(A) = P(A)P(Bᶜ) forces P(Bᶜ)=1, i.e. P(B)=0 — so the 'closure' conclusion is false for anything but genuine product-form independence.

title: The discrete uniform law（離散均勻律）is a derived counting formula, valid only when Ω is finite and equal likelihood has been separately justified
source_quote: Discrete uniform law – Assume Ω consists of n equally likely elements – Assume A consists of k elements. P(A) = [handwritten annotation] k · 1/n. [handwritten annotation, inserted above the first bullet] finite (slide p13)
irreducible_premises: Ω is finite with n elements — the instructor's handwritten insertion of 'finite' is essential
All n outcomes are assigned equal probability, which is a modelling assumption about the experiment
Finite additivity over disjoint singletons
Normalization P(Ω) = 1
An event A is a subset containing k of those elements
derivation_chain: Decompose Ω into its n singletons, which are disjoint, and apply finite additivity to get P(Ω) = Σ P({sᵢ}).
Impose equal likelihood, so all n terms are a common value p, and normalization gives np = 1, hence p = 1/n — the per-outcome probability is deduced, not posited.
Decompose the event A into its k singletons and apply finite additivity again to get P(A) as a sum of k terms.
Substitute p = 1/n to obtain P(A) = k·(1/n) = k/n, so the uniform law is a counting consequence of the axioms plus the equal-likelihood assumption.

Verify on the two-roll tetrahedral die: n = 16 equally likely pairs, and the event X = 1 contains k = 4 of them, giving P(X = 1) = 4·(1/16) = 1/4, while Z = min(X,Y) = 2 contains k = 5 cells, giving 5/16.
By the equal-assignment premise, each of the n outcomes has an unknown common probability q.
Substituting q = 1/n gives P(A) = k/n, i.e. probability = (count of A)/(count of Ω), which is why the entire rest of the lecture is about counting and nothing else.
assumptions: Ω is finite, so 1/n is a positive number and finite additivity suffices
Equal likelihood is warranted by the physical symmetry of the experiment rather than by convenience
The event A is counted at the same granularity as the elements of Ω
Ω is finite (or the model is reduced to a finite equally-likely set)
The elements listed as 'outcomes' are genuinely equally likely under the underlying model

If the outcomes are not in fact equally likely — a biased die, or a Ω whose elements were formed by merging unequal cases — then k/n is simply the wrong number and the error equals the discrepancy between the true masses and 1/n summed over A.
If A is counted at a coarser granularity than Ω, e.g. counting the value of Z rather than the (X,Y) cells that realize it, k is undercounted and P(A) comes out too small — P(Z = 2) is 5/16, not 1/16.

In the die example on slide p04 both numerator 6! and denominator 6^6 are counts of ordered 6-tuples — the correctness depends entirely on that match.
If Ω is infinite or continuous, n is not a finite number and k/n is undefined; the counting reduction has no meaning and a density-based law is required instead.

title: Conditioning（條件化）replaces the original probability law with a new one obtained by restricting to B and rescaling by P(B)
source_quote: Definition of conditional probability. P(A | B) = "probability of A, given that B occurred". P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), defined only when P(B) > 0 (slide p03)
irreducible_premises: A probability law P is already defined on the events of a sample space Ω and satisfies nonnegativity, P(Ω)=1, and additivity on disjoint events
Observing that event B occurred rules out every outcome outside B, so outcomes in B^c must receive zero probability in the revised model
The information 'B occurred' carries no evidence about the relative likelihoods of outcomes inside B, so those relative weights must be preserved
A revised assignment is only a probability law if the total probability it assigns to B equals 1
P(B) > 0, otherwise the conditioning event has no probability mass to renormalize

By the premise that relative weights inside B are unchanged, the surviving 6 outcomes must stay equally likely to one another, so each gets the same new value c — the handwritten annotation on p02 records c = 1/6.
By the premise that the revised law must assign total probability 1, impose 6c = 1, i.e. divide every surviving weight by the original P(B) = 6/12; this is the rescaling step.
Apply the rescaled law to A: only the 2 outcomes in A ∩ B survive, giving P(A | B) = (2/12)/(6/12) = 2/6 = 1/3, exactly as annotated on p02–p03.

The underlying law P on Ω is a legitimate probability law before conditioning

title: Bayes' rule（貝氏定理）inverts the direction of conditioning: it turns a forward model P(B | A_i) plus prior beliefs P(A_i) into revised posterior beliefs P(A_i | B)
source_quote: Bayes' rule. Partition of sample space into A_1, A_2, A_3. Have P(A_i), for every i — initial "beliefs". Have P(B | A_i), for every i. revised "beliefs," given that B occurred: P(A_i | B) = P(A_i)P(B | A_i) / Σ_j P(A_j)P(B | A_j). [handwritten annotation] P(A_i | B) = P(A_i ∩ B)/P(B) (slide p09)
irreducible_premises: The definition of conditional probability P(A_i | B) = P(A_i ∩ B)/P(B), valid because P(B) > 0
The multiplication rule P(A_i ∩ B) = P(A_i) P(B | A_i)
The total probability theorem P(B) = Σ_j P(A_j) P(B | A_j)
A_1, A_2, A_3, ... partition Ω, so exactly one cause A_i is in force and the posteriors must sum to one
The prior beliefs P(A_i) and the forward model P(B | A_i) are both given as inputs, separately from the observation B
derivation_chain: Start from the definition premise and write the target posterior as the ratio P(A_i | B) = P(A_i ∩ B)/P(B) — the red annotation on p09.
Replace the numerator using the multiplication rule premise: P(A_i ∩ B) = P(A_i) P(B | A_i), so the numerator is prior times likelihood, both of which are given inputs.
Replace the denominator using the total probability premise: P(B) = Σ_j P(A_j) P(B | A_j), which is also built entirely from the same given inputs.

Combine steps 2 and 3 to obtain the boxed rule P(A_i | B) = P(A_i)P(B | A_i) / Σ_j P(A_j)P(B | A_j); the denominator is the sum of all numerators, so by the partition premise the posteriors automatically sum to one.

Read the result as the inference direction of p10: the model arrow goes A_i → B via P(B | A_i), and Bayes' rule reverses it, B → A_i via P(A_i | B) — 'a systematic approach for incorporating new evidence'. The p06 radar instance gives P(A | B) = (0.05 × 0.99)/0.1445 = 0.34.
assumptions: P(B) > 0, i.e. the observed evidence has positive probability under the model
The A_i are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so the normalizing sum really covers all candidate causes
Priors P(A_i) and likelihoods P(B | A_i) are specified before and independently of observing B
failure_modes: Confusing the two directions of conditioning — reporting P(B | A_i) as if it were P(A_i | B) — is the base-rate error the radar example on p06 is built to expose: the detector is excellent, P(B | A) = 0.99, yet after an alarm P(A | B) is only 0.34, so treating 0.99 as the posterior overstates the answer by roughly a factor of three.

If a true cause is left out of the partition, the denominator Σ_j P(A_j)P(B | A_j) is too small and every posterior is inflated by the same factor, yet they still sum to one, so the arithmetic gives no warning that the model is wrong.

If the evidence is impossible under every listed cause, all P(B | A_j) = 0 makes the denominator zero and the posterior undefined — the rule cannot update on evidence its own model assigns probability zero, and no renormalization can rescue it.

title: The multiplication rule（乘法法則）builds the probability of an intersection as a product of one unconditional and successively conditional factors along a tree path
source_quote: The multiplication rule. P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B) = P(A) P(B | A). P(A^c ∩ B ∩ C^c) = [handwritten annotation] = P(A^c ∩ B) P(C^c | A^c ∩ B) = P(A^c) · P(B | A^c) P(C^c | A^c ∩ B); P(A_1 ∩ A_2 ∩ ... ∩ A_n) = P(A_1) ∏_{i=2}^{n} P(A_i | A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_{i-1}) (slide p07)
irreducible_premises: The definition P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) holds whenever P(B) > 0
Multiplying both sides of that definition by P(B) is an identity, not a new assumption
Intersection is commutative, so A ∩ B may be factored by conditioning on either event
Intersection is associative, so an n-fold intersection can be grouped as (A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_{i-1}) ∩ A_i
Every prefix event A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_{i-1} has strictly positive probability so each conditional factor exists
derivation_chain: Take the definition premise and clear the denominator: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B).

By the commutativity premise, repeat the same clearing with the roles of A and B swapped to get the second printed form P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B | A); the two products must be equal because they describe the same set.
For three events, use the associativity premise to view A^c ∩ B ∩ C^c as (A^c ∩ B) ∩ C^c and apply step 1 once: P(A^c ∩ B ∩ C^c) = P(A^c ∩ B) P(C^c | A^c ∩ B).

Apply step 1 again to the remaining pair P(A^c ∩ B) = P(A^c) P(B | A^c), giving the handwritten three-factor product that reads exactly as the branch probabilities along the highlighted tree path on p07.

Iterate the same substitution n − 1 times, each time peeling off the last event, and the positivity premise guarantees every factor is defined: P(A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_n) = P(A_1) ∏_{i=2}^n P(A_i | A_1 ∩ ... ∩ A_{i-1}) — the blue annotation.
assumptions: Each conditioning event in the chain has positive probability
The ordering of events used to factor the intersection is fixed before multiplying; any order is legal but the factors must match that order
Each factor is conditioned on the full history of the preceding events, not on a single predecessor
failure_modes: Conditioning each factor on only the immediately preceding event instead of the whole prefix silently assumes a Markov-type property: writing P(C^c | B) in place of P(C^c | A^c ∩ B) on p07 replaces a tree-branch probability with a different number and the product no longer equals the leaf probability.

Multiplying unconditional probabilities, P(A) P(B), instead of P(A) P(B | A) assumes independence; in the radar model of p06 that would give 0.05 × 0.1445 ≈ 0.0072 instead of the correct 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.0495, an error of nearly a factor of seven.
If some prefix event has probability zero the corresponding conditional factor is undefined; the product must then be assigned zero directly, since any attempt to evaluate the factor divides by zero.

title: Independence of a collection requires the product identity for every subset of indices, so pairwise independence（兩兩獨立）is strictly weaker
source_quote: Definition: Events A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ are called independent if: P(A_i ∩ A_j ∩ ⋯ ∩ A_m) = P(A_i)P(A_j) ⋯ P(A_m) for any distinct indices i, j, …, m. … H₁, H₂, and C are pairwise independent, but not independent (slides p07, p08)
irreducible_premises: The product identity is imposed separately on each subset of distinct indices; it is a family of 2ⁿ − n − 1 equations, not one equation
The intuitive content is that information on some of the events does not change probabilities related to the remaining events
Equal-likelihood assignment on {HH, HT, TH, TT} with probability 1/4 each
Two-event independence of H₁ and H₂ does not constrain any event defined jointly on both tosses
derivation_chain: Write out the definition for n = 3, using the every-subset premise: three pairwise equations plus the separate triple equation P(A₁∩A₂∩A₃) = P(A₁)P(A₂)P(A₃).

Take the slide's counterexample: two independent fair tosses, H₁ = first is H, H₂ = second is H, C = the two tosses had the same result = {HH, TT}, so P(H₁) = P(H₂) = P(C) = 1/2 under the equal-likelihood premise.
Verify the three pairwise equations: P(H₁∩C) = P(H₁∩H₂) = 1/4 = (1/2)(1/2) = P(H₁)P(C), and symmetrically for H₂ and C, so all three pairs are independent.
Test the triple: P(H₁∩H₂∩C) = P(HH) = 1/4, while P(H₁)P(H₂)P(C) = 1/8 — the two differ by 1/8, so the collection is not independent.

Read the same failure in conditional form: P(C|H₁) = P(H₂|H₁) = 1/2 = P(C), but P(C|H₁∩H₂) = 1 ≠ 1/2, so joint information on two events does change the third — exactly what the intuitive premise forbids.
assumptions: All events are defined on one common sample space with a single law
The collection is checked subset by subset, including all higher-order intersections
In the counterexample the two tosses are fair and independent
failure_modes: Certifying a collection as independent after checking only pairs: for H₁, H₂, C the triple probability is 1/4 instead of 1/8, so any computation multiplying all three marginals is off by a factor of 2.

Using pairwise independence to justify 'information on some events does not affect the rest': here P(C|H₁∩H₂) = 1 while P(C) = 1/2, so a conditional forecast built on pairwise checks can be wrong by 1/2 and can even mistake a certainty for a coin flip.
Checking only the single full-collection identity and skipping subsets: P(A₁∩A₂∩A₃)=P(A₁)P(A₂)P(A₃) can hold while a pair fails, so subsets of the collection then cannot be multiplied out.

title: System reliability（可靠度）: independence of unit states turns series connectivity into a product of pᵢ and parallel connectivity into 1 − ∏(1 − pᵢ)
source_quote: Reliability. pᵢ: probability that unit i is "up". independent units. probability that system is "up"? [handwritten annotation] Uᵢ: ith unit up; U₁,U₂,…,Uₙ independent; Fᵢ: ith unit down ⇒ Fᵢ independent. P(system up) = P(U₁∩U₂∩U₃) = P(U₁)P(U₂)P(U₃) = p₁p₂p₃. P(system is up) = P(U₁∪U₂∪U₃) = 1 − P(F₁∩F₂∩F₃) = 1 − P(F₁)P(F₂)P(F₃) = 1 − (1−p₁)(1−p₂)(1−p₃) (slide p09)
irreducible_premises: Each unit i has a state event Uᵢ with P(Uᵢ) = pᵢ
The events U₁, …, Uₙ are independent as a collection, so every subset multiplies
Closure of independence under complements, extended to the collection: the down-events Fᵢ = Uᵢᶜ are independent too
De Morgan / complement identity P(U₁∪⋯∪Uₙ) = 1 − P(F₁∩⋯∩Fₙ)
Series connectivity means all units must be up; parallel connectivity means at least one must be up
derivation_chain: Translate the wiring diagram into events, using the connectivity premise: series 'system up' = U₁∩U₂∩U₃, parallel 'system up' = U₁∪U₂∪U₃.
For the series case apply collection independence directly to the intersection: P(U₁∩U₂∩U₃) = P(U₁)P(U₂)P(U₃) = p₁p₂p₃.
For the parallel case the union is not a product, so convert it with the complement identity: P(U₁∪U₂∪U₃) = 1 − P(F₁∩F₂∩F₃).
Use closure under complements to declare F₁, F₂, F₃ independent, then multiply: P(F₁∩F₂∩F₃) = (1−p₁)(1−p₂)(1−p₃).
Combine: P(parallel system up) = 1 − (1−p₁)(1−p₂)(1−p₃), which is at least maxᵢ pᵢ, while the series answer p₁p₂p₃ is at most minᵢ pᵢ.
assumptions: Units fail independently — no shared power supply, shared load, or common environmental shock
Each unit is strictly two-state, up or down, with no partial or intermittent state
The network reduces cleanly into series and parallel blocks so the events are pure intersections and unions of the Uᵢ
failure_modes: Correlated failures: if the units share a common cause, the true series reliability exceeds p₁p₂p₃ (failures coincide) and the true parallel reliability falls below 1 − ∏(1−pᵢ), so the independence formula misstates the risk in the direction that matters for design.

Multiplying the union directly, i.e. computing P(U₁∪U₂∪U₃) as p₁p₂p₃: this returns the series answer for a parallel network — with p₁=p₂=p₃=0.9 it gives 0.729 instead of 0.999, understating reliability by 0.27.

Applying the product step when the collection is only pairwise independent: the three-way identity P(F₁∩F₂∩F₃)=P(F₁)P(F₂)P(F₃) is exactly the equation pairwise independence fails to supply, so the parallel formula has no justification.

title: The king's sibling puzzle: independent child genders fix the prior, but the conditioning protocol（觀測程序）fixes the answer
source_quote: The king's sibling. The king comes from a family of two children. What is the probability that his sibling is female? [handwritten annotation] 1/2 crossed out, replaced by 2/3. P(boy) = P(girl) = 1/2, independent. boys have precedence. BB 1/4, BG 1/4, GB 1/4, GG 1/4. • till 1 boy ⇒ P(G) = 1; • till 2 boys ⇒ P(G) = 0 (slide p10)
irreducible_premises: Each child is a boy or girl with probability 1/2, and the two children's genders are independent, giving BB, BG, GB, GG each probability 1/4
Conditional probability requires the conditioning event to be specified as a set of outcomes, not as a verbal fact
Different data-generating protocols map the same verbal fact to different conditioning events
'Boys have precedence' — the king exists iff the family contains at least one boy
derivation_chain: Assign the prior from independence and fairness: the four outcomes BB, BG, GB, GG each have probability 1/4.
Under the precedence premise, translate 'there is a king' into the event {BB, BG, GB}, of probability 3/4, and note this is the green loop drawn on the slide.
Condition: the sibling is female in the two outcomes BG and GB, so P(sibling female | at least one boy) = (1/4 + 1/4)/(3/4) = 2/3, not the crossed-out 1/2.

Change only the protocol, keeping the same independent prior: if the family kept having children until it had 1 boy, the boy is the last child and every earlier child is a girl, so P(G) = 1; if it kept going until 2 boys, the sibling is the other boy and P(G) = 0.

Conclude that the prior on genders is not what determines the answer — the answer ranges over 0, 1/2, 2/3, 1 as the conditioning event changes, so the protocol must be stated before any number is computed.
assumptions: Genders are independent and equally likely, with no twins and no biological correlation
The stopping or selection rule that produced the observation is fully specified
The king's own gender is fixed as male by the setup, so it carries no additional information beyond defining the conditioning event

Reusing the 2/3 answer under a stopping rule: with 'children until 1 boy' the correct answer is 1 and with 'until 2 boys' it is 0, so the same verbal question is off by 1/3 or 2/3 depending on the protocol.

title: The basic counting principle（計數基本原理）multiplies stage counts, and it is valid only when the NUMBER of choices at each stage is the same no matter what was chosen earlier
source_quote: Basic counting principle. • r stages • n_i choices at stage i. Number of choices is: [handwritten annotation] n₁ · n₂ ··· n_r  [handwritten annotation on the tree: 4, 12, 24 = 4·3·2; r = 3, n₁ = 4, n₂ = 3, n₃ = 2] (slide p02)
irreducible_premises: A composite object is built by a fixed sequence of r stages
Each distinct sequence of stage-choices yields a distinct object, and every object arises from exactly one such sequence
At stage i the number of available choices is n_i, a constant independent of the choices made at stages 1..i-1
Counting a finite set can be done by counting the leaves of the construction tree
derivation_chain: Represent the construction as a tree whose depth-i nodes are the partial objects after i stages (premise: staged construction).
By the constant-count premise, every node at depth i-1 has exactly n_i children, so the node count multiplies by n_i at each level: 4, then 4·3 = 12, then 4·3·2 = 24 in the shirts/ties/jackets tree.
Hence the number of leaves at depth r is n₁ n₂ ··· n_r.

By the bijection premise (each object ↔ exactly one leaf), the number of objects equals that product; permutations follow immediately as n(n-1)(n-2)···1 = n! and the subsets of {1,...,n} as 2·2···2 = 2^n by taking 'in or out' as each stage.
assumptions: The count n_i at each stage does not depend on earlier choices (the identity of the available options may change, the count may not)
The stage-sequence → object map is a bijection: no object is reachable by two different sequences and none is unreachable
The number of stages r is fixed in advance
failure_modes: If the number of choices at a stage depends on earlier choices, the product is wrong. Example: license plates with 2 letters then 3 digits give 26·26·10·10·10, but with repetition prohibited the counts fall to 26·25·10·9·8 — the principle still applies there only because the *count* drops by a fixed amount each stage; if instead the available count varied with WHICH earlier item was picked (e.g. 'pick a divisor of the first number'), no single n_i exists and the product silently over- or under-counts.
If different stage-sequences produce the same object, the product over-counts by exactly the multiplicity of that collapse — this is the defect that combinations must repair by dividing by k!.

source_quote: Combinations. Definition: (n choose k): number of k-element subsets of a given n-element set. • Two ways of constructing an ordered sequence of k distinct items: — Choose the k items one at a time — Choose k items, then order them. The number of orderings of k distinct items is k! (permutations)
A k-element subset carries no order: it is one object regardless of how its members are listed
Two correct counts of the SAME set must be equal (the double-counting identity)
derivation_chain: Route 1: build an ordered sequence of k distinct items one slot at a time; by the counting principle this gives n(n-1)···(n-k+1) = n!/(n-k)! sequences.
Route 2: first choose the underlying k-element subset in (n choose k) ways, then arrange those k items in k! orders; by the counting principle this gives (n choose k)·k! sequences.
Both routes count exactly the same set of ordered k-sequences, so by the double-counting premise (n choose k)·k! = n!/(n-k)!.

The same identity fixes the boundary cases via the convention 0! = 1: (n choose n) = n!/(n!0!) = 1 and (n choose 0) = n!/(0!n!) = 1, the single subset being the whole set and the empty set.

The target objects are unordered subsets, and 0 ≤ k ≤ n
0! = 1 by convention, so the endpoint cases are consistent

title: A binomial probability（二項機率）factors into one probability times one count because every k-head sequence has the same probability p^k(1-p)^{n-k}
source_quote: Binomial coefficient (n choose k) → Binomial probabilities. • n ≥ 1 independent coin tosses; P(H) = p • P(particular sequence) = [handwritten annotation] p^{#heads}(1-p)^{#tails} • P(particular k−head sequence) = [handwritten annotation] p^k(1-p)^{n-k}. P(k heads) = (n choose k) p^k (1-p)^{n-k} (slide p07)
irreducible_premises: The n tosses are independent
Each toss has the same P(H) = p (identical marginals)
Finite additivity of probability over disjoint events
The number of length-n sequences with exactly k heads is (n choose k)
derivation_chain: By independence and identical marginals, the probability of one specific sequence is the product of its per-toss probabilities, e.g. P(HTTHHH) = p(1-p)(1-p)ppp = p^4(1-p)^2.
That product depends only on how many heads and tails occur, not on their positions, so every sequence with exactly k heads has the identical probability p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
The event {k heads} is the disjoint union of all such sequences, so by additivity P(k heads) = (number of k-head sequences) · p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
Choosing which k of the n slots hold the heads is exactly choosing a k-element subset of the slots, giving (n choose k) sequences, hence P(k heads) = (n choose k) p^k (1-p)^{n-k}.

Conditioning on B = {3 heads in 10} therefore induces a uniform law on the 3-head sequences, since each has the same p^3(1-p)^7; the conditional answer reduces to counting: P(A|B) = #(A∩B)/#B = (8 choose 1)/(10 choose 3) = 8/(10 choose 3).
assumptions: Tosses are independent AND identically distributed with the same p
n is fixed in advance, not chosen based on the results
0 ≤ k ≤ n
failure_modes: If the tosses are dependent (e.g. the coin is drawn once from a bag of biased coins and reused), sequences with the same k no longer share a probability, the factorisation collapses, and multiplying by (n choose k) attaches the wrong common weight to every term. The same defect breaks the counting shortcut on slide p09: the conditional law on B is uniform only because every 3-head sequence shares probability p^3(1-p)^7.

If p varies across tosses, P(sequence) is a product of different p_i and depends on WHICH positions are heads; the count (n choose k) then multiplies a non-representative single term and the result can be off in either direction.

If n is not fixed but determined by the data (e.g. stop at the third head), the set of possible sequences is not all length-n strings, the count (n choose k) includes impossible sequences, and the probabilities no longer sum to 1 over k.

title: The multinomial coefficient（多項式係數）counts partitions by dividing n! by the internal orderings each group absorbs
source_quote: Partitions. • n ≥ 1 distinct items; r ≥ 1 persons give n_i items to person i — here n₁,...,n_r are given nonnegative integers — with n₁ + ··· + n_r = n • Ordering n items: [handwritten annotation] n! — Deal n_i to each person i, and then order [handwritten annotation] c · n₁! n₂! ··· n_r! = n!. number of partitions = n!/(n₁! n₂! ··· n_r!) (multinomial coefficient) (slide p10)
irreducible_premises: The n items are distinct and the r persons (groups) are distinguishable
The group sizes n_i are fixed nonnegative integers with n₁ + ··· + n_r = n
The number of orderings of m distinct items is m!
The basic counting principle, applied to a two-route construction of one ordered list of all n items
derivation_chain: Route 1: order all n items in a single line — by permutations this can be done in n! ways.

Route 2: build the same line in stages — first choose the partition (call the unknown number of partitions c), assigning n_i items to the block of n_i consecutive slots belonging to person i, then order within each block in n_i! ways.
By the counting principle, route 2 yields c · n₁! n₂! ··· n_r! lists, and by double counting this equals n!.
Therefore c = n!/(n₁! n₂! ··· n_r!): each n_i! in the denominator is exactly the internal ordering of group i that the partition deliberately ignores.
The binomial coefficient is the case r = 2 with n₁ = k, n₂ = n-k, recovering n!/(k!(n-k)!) — combinations are a partition into 'chosen' and 'not chosen'.
assumptions: Items are distinguishable and groups are labelled (person 1 vs person 2 is a different partition)
The sizes n_i are prescribed in advance and sum to n
Order within a group is irrelevant

If the group sizes are not fixed but free to vary, the formula answers a different question and must be summed over all admissible size vectors; using one term understates the total.

If items are indistinguishable, the ordered-line route has fewer than n! distinct lists, the double-counting identity c · ∏ n_i! = n! is false, and the quotient no longer counts anything. title: A counting-based probability is only as good as the sample space chosen, so switching to a coarser equally likely space can replace a huge count with a short product
source_quote: Example: 52-card deck, dealt (fairly) to four players. Find P(each player gets an ace). • Outcomes are: [handwritten annotation] partition, equally likely — number of outcomes: 52!/(13!13!13!13!) (slide p11) ... A smart solution: Stack the deck, aces on top. [handwritten annotation] 39/51 · 26/50 · 13/49 = .105 (slide p12)
irreducible_premises: The discrete uniform law: P(A) = |A|/|Ω| when outcomes are equally likely
The same physical experiment admits several different sample spaces (full partitions, or just the relative placement of the four aces)
A fair deal means every partition of the 52 distinct cards into four labelled 13-card hands is equally likely
Symmetry: under a fair deal, an ace is equally likely to land in any of the remaining slots
derivation_chain: Take Ω = all partitions into four 13-card hands; by the multinomial count |Ω| = 52!/(13!13!13!13!), and by fairness these are equally likely.

Count the favourable partitions by staged construction: distribute the four aces one per player in 4·3·2·1 ways, then distribute the remaining 48 cards as 48!/(12!12!12!12!), giving the ratio [4·3·2·1·48!/(12!^4)]/[52!/(13!^4)].

Alternatively pick the coarser space: stack the deck with the aces on top and ask only where each successive ace lands. Given the first ace's pile, 39 of the remaining 51 positions lie in other piles; then 26 of 50; then 13 of 49.

By the counting principle over these three stages and the uniform law on this coarser but still equally likely space, P = (39/51)(26/50)(13/49) ≈ .105 — the same number, obtained without ever evaluating a factorial.
Both routes agree because each is a correct uniform-law computation on its own consistent sample space; the choice of space is a modelling decision, not a mathematical one.
assumptions: The deal is fair, so the chosen sample space really is equally likely
The coarser description (positions of the four aces relative to piles) preserves equal likelihood by symmetry
Numerator and denominator are counted in the same sample space
failure_modes: Coarsening a sample space usually destroys equal likelihood: lumping outcomes into 'each player gets an ace / not' gives two outcomes but not probability 1/2. The stacking argument is legitimate only because the symmetry of a fair deal makes each remaining position equally likely for the next ace — without that symmetry check the shortcut yields a confidently wrong number.

Mixing spaces mid-calculation — counting favourable cases as ordered deals but total cases as partitions — produces a ratio inflated or deflated by a factorial factor with no visible symptom, since both numbers are plausible-looking large integers.

If the deal were not fair (a stacked or partially dealt deck), the partitions are not equally likely, |A|/|Ω| no longer applies, and both the factorial route and the 39/51·26/50·13/49 route are invalid even though both still evaluate to .105.
